Whether Carmen Lomas Garza is creating small paintings and illustrations or large public artworks—such as Baile, a copper cutout of a traditional Mexican dance in the San Francisco International Airport—she is ______ direct experience, drawing from memories of her childhood in Texas or details of her current surroundings in California.

Whether chef Amara Osei is developing a five-course tasting menu or a single street-food dish, she is ______ the seasonal produce of her grandmother's garden, adapting recipes to reflect whatever vegetables and herbs are ready to harvest that week.

Whether composing a symphony for a full orchestra or a simple lullaby for solo piano, composer Henrik Larsen is ______ the folk melodies he heard sung in his grandparents' village, often weaving fragments of those tunes into his own original themes.

Whether designing a modest footbridge or a sprawling museum complex, architect Teodora Voss is ______ the eroded canyon walls near her hometown, repeatedly echoing their layered, sweeping curves in the buildings' facades.

Whether corresponding with strangers or close friends, poet Miriam Okafor is ______ the handwritten letters her mother saved from decades of family correspondence, often borrowing a phrase or an image directly from their fading pages.

Whether shooting a low-budget short or a big-studio feature, filmmaker Diego Reyes is ______ the recurring dream he had as a child of a house whose rooms rearranged themselves overnight, a dream he has now reimagined in nearly every film he has made.
Disproving the common misconception of Native art as ______, the painters whose work appears in the collection at the National Museum of the American Indian employ a range of styles.

There are artists working in the traditional arts of their specific tribal communities, artists working in European modernist or American abstract expressionist art traditions, and artists blending various traditions into something wholly new.
Disproving the common misconception of a country's regional cuisine as ______, the dishes served across its provinces reveal sharp differences in spice, technique, and staple ingredient.

Coastal towns favor light broths and raw seafood, mountain villages rely on slow-braised meats and preserved vegetables, and the capital blends both traditions with imported spices from centuries of trade.

Disproving the common misconception of protest music as ______, historians point to recordings that range from quiet acoustic ballads to full orchestral arrangements to sparse electronic tracks, each shaped by the political moment and available technology of its decade.

Disproving the common misconception of the species' nesting habits as ______, field biologists have documented colonies that build elevated stick platforms, others that burrow into riverbanks, and still others that simply scrape a shallow depression in open sand.

Disproving the common misconception of the early labor movement as ______, archival records reveal factions that pursued shop-floor bargaining, others that lobbied for national legislation, and still others that organized entirely separate cooperative enterprises.

Disproving the common misconception of coral reef fish communities as ______, marine surveys have found some reefs dominated by a handful of generalist species while neighboring reefs, only a few kilometers away, support dozens of specialized species found nowhere else.
Recent measurements of the mass of the boson (a subatomic particle) were notable not only for the mere fact that the particle's mass differed from expectations but for the ______ of that difference.
The measured mass of the boson was seven standard deviations higher than predicted by the standard model of particle physics.

Recent measurements of the average temperature of the lake bed were notable not only for the fact that the reading differed from expectations but for the ______ of that difference: the measured temperature was nearly nine degrees higher than models based on decades of prior data had predicted.

Astronomers who tracked the star's sudden brightening were struck not merely by the change itself but by the ______ of that change: within six hours, the star's luminosity had increased by a factor of nearly two hundred.

Economists reviewing the new employment survey were surprised less by the direction of the shift than by the ______ of it: the number of workers who changed industries within a single year was nearly triple the historical average.

Glaciologists monitoring the retreat of the ice sheet were concerned not simply that it was retreating but by the ______ of the retreat: satellite images showed the glacier's edge had moved back nearly a kilometer in a single decade.

Analysts reviewing the firm's quarterly report were less concerned with the fact of a loss than with the ______ of that loss: revenue had fallen by more than sixty percent compared with the same quarter the previous year.
Birds sing to communicate over potentially great distances.

For this reason, many researchers believe that birds in densely vegetated habitats generally sing at lower frequencies than birds living in comparatively sparse habitats, since dense vegetation tends to ______ the distance that high-frequency sounds can travel.
Ships navigating the strait rely on radar because heavy fog tends to ______ the distance at which lookouts can spot approaching vessels, sometimes reducing visibility to less than one hundred meters.

Engineers designing the new headphones found that soft foam padding tends to ______ the range of low-frequency sounds that reach the wearer's ear, blocking most engine noise while leaving voices audible.

Botanists studying the shrub found that shallow, rocky soil tends to ______ how far its roots can spread, forcing the plant to rely on a dense network of surface roots rather than a single deep taproot.

Submarine communication is difficult because seawater tends to ______ the range over which low-frequency radio signals can travel, forcing crews to rely on extremely long antennas or sound-based systems instead.

Ornithologists tracking the songbirds found that a lack of stopover wetlands tends to ______ how far the birds can migrate in a single season, sometimes stranding exhausted flocks well short of their usual breeding grounds.
The following text is from Betty Smith's 1943 novel A Tree Grows in Brooklyn.
Francie, a young girl, visits the library often.
Francie thought that all the books in the world were in that library and she had a plan about reading all the books in the world.
She was reading a book a day in alphabetical order and not skipping the dry ones.
She remembered that the first author had been Abbott.
She had been reading a book a day for a long time now and she was still in the B's.
Already she had read about bees and buffaloes, Bermuda vacations and Byzantine architecture.
For her enthusiasm, she had to admit that some of the B's had been hard going.
But Francie was a reader.
The following text is from a short story.
Every summer, Malik decided he would learn to identify every bird that visited his grandmother's yard, working entirely from a battered field guide missing its back cover.
He started with the sparrows because they were the plainest and, he reasoned, the easiest to get out of the way.
By July he had moved on to warblers, squinting through binoculars at flickers of yellow in the highest branches, filling a notebook with crossed-out guesses.
Some mornings the birds refused to show themselves at all, and Malik simply sat on the porch steps and waited, sure that patience was the last skill the guide couldn't teach him.
The following text is from a novel.
Rosa had promised herself she would repair every chair in her late uncle's workshop before selling the building, even the three-legged ones warped beyond any obvious use.
She learned to steam bend ash by ruining four strips of wood and consulting a library book so old its spine cracked when opened.
Neighbors dropped by to ask when the workshop would finally be listed, and Rosa answered vaguely, already sanding down another armrest.
By the time she finished the last chair, the for-sale sign had gathered a season's worth of dust in the hall closet.
The following text is from a memoir.
My father decided, the winter I turned nine, that our family would learn every constellation visible from the back field before spring.

He photocopied star charts at the library and taped them to the refrigerator, and some nights we stood in the cold long after our fingers went numb, arguing about which faint cluster was Cassiopeia and which was simply a smudge on the chart.
He never explained why it mattered so much, only that we would finish what he'd started, chart by chart, until the refrigerator was bare.
Delphine had never run more than a mile before she signed up for the marathon, a decision she made mostly to prove something to herself rather than to anyone watching.
She trained before dawn so no one would see her walking half the route, kept a log of every blister and every mile she managed to finish, and refused every excuse her body offered her to quit.
On race day, she crossed the line four hours after the winner, smiling as though she had won something no clock could measure.
Old Mr. Petrov decided that before he died he would translate his grandfather's diary, page by page, from a dialect that only a handful of people still spoke.
He spent his afternoons hunched over a dictionary held together with tape, filling notebook after notebook with tentative English phrases he crossed out and rewrote.
His daughter offered to hire a professional translator, but he waved her off each time, insisting that the words meant nothing unless he found them himself.
The people of medieval Europe have traditionally been seen as uninterested in cleanliness and hygiene, but modern research has shown that this is largely a myth.
According to historian Eleanor Janega, most medieval towns in Europe had at least one public bathhouse, which often offered both full-immersion baths and—more affordably—steam baths.
While such amenities were available mainly to town dwellers, regular bathing in rivers and streams or daily sponge baths at home were common practices throughout medieval Europe.
Nineteenth-century factory workers have traditionally been seen as having no access to printed reading material, but modern research has shown that this is largely an oversimplification.
According to historian Owen Bracewell, most industrial towns had at least one subscription library that circulated inexpensive serialized novels among workers.
While such libraries were concentrated mainly in larger mill towns, informal book-sharing among coworkers and readings aloud during breaks were common practices throughout the industrial regions.
Rural households in the early twentieth century have traditionally been seen as isolated from national news, but modern research has shown that this view is largely mistaken.
According to historian Priya Chandran, most rural counties had at least one shared radio set, often housed in a general store or town hall.
While such radios were owned mainly by a handful of wealthier merchants, informal gatherings to listen to broadcasts were common practices throughout rural communities.
Enslaved artisans in the antebellum South have traditionally been seen as excluded from any formal recognition of their craft, but modern research complicates that picture.
According to historian Marcus Dell, several enslaved potters and blacksmiths had their work purchased and displayed at regional fairs under their own names.
While such recognition was granted mainly by a small number of sympathetic fair organizers, the sale and use of their crafted goods was common practice throughout the region.
Medieval European peasants have traditionally been seen as having no access to spices beyond salt, but modern research complicates that assumption.
According to historian Ingrid Solheim, most manor households kept at least a small store of pepper or mustard seed, often purchased at seasonal markets.
While such spices were affordable mainly to peasants with a modest surplus income, growing and using local herbs for flavoring was a common practice throughout the peasantry.
Colonial-era sailors have traditionally been seen as entirely illiterate, but modern research has revised that assumption.
According to historian Felix Amaro, most merchant ships carried at least one crew member capable of reading navigational charts and basic correspondence.
While full literacy was common mainly among officers and a handful of experienced hands, informal instruction in reading simple logbook entries was practiced throughout many crews.
When classical pianist Martha Argerich performs, it appears as if the music is coming to her spontaneously.
She's highly skilled technically, but because of how freely she plays and her willingness to take risks, she seems relaxed and natural.
Her apparent ease, however, is due to a tremendous amount of preparation.
Despite Argerich's experience and virtuosity, she never takes for granted that she knows a piece of music.
Instead, she approaches the music as if encountering it for the first time and tries to understand it anew.
When gymnast Ines Duarte competes, her routines look almost casual, as if the flips and turns cost her no effort at all.
She has extraordinary natural flexibility, but her apparent looseness on the beam comes from years of repeating each transition thousands of times until her body no longer has to think about it.
Despite her experience, Duarte still rehearses every routine at quarter speed before competitions, treating even familiar sequences as though a single misplaced habit could still creep back in.
When chess grandmaster Yusuf Karimov plays, his moves seem to arrive instantly, as though he simply senses the right square without calculation.
He is naturally quick, but his apparent speed is the product of thousands of hours spent memorizing patterns from historical games.
Despite decades of experience, Karimov still studies each opponent's past matches beforehand, refusing to assume that instinct alone will carry him through an unfamiliar position.
When chef Odalys Ferreira plates a dish during a live cooking demonstration, her hands move so smoothly that the entire process seems unplanned.
She has a natural feel for flavor, but her calm, unhurried pace on stage comes from rehearsing the same sequence of cuts and plating motions dozens of times beforehand.
Even after years of demonstrations, Ferreira still times a full practice run the morning of each show, unwilling to trust that familiarity alone will keep her steady under the lights.
When violinist Theo Marchetti performs a concerto, his fingers seem to find each note without hesitation, as though the piece has always simply lived in his hands.
He has considerable natural talent, but his apparent ease comes from slow, deliberate practice sessions in which he isolates and repeats the most difficult passages far more often than the easy ones.
Even with a piece he has performed dozens of times, Marchetti still runs through it at half tempo before a concert, refusing to assume his fingers will remember it on their own.
When public speaker Naledi Mokoena delivers a keynote, she seems to speak entirely off the cuff, pausing and gesturing as though the words are occurring to her in the moment.

She has a naturally warm stage presence, but her apparent spontaneity is the result of rehearsing the same talk dozens of times in front of a mirror until each pause feels natural rather than scripted.
Even for talks she has given many times before, Mokoena still rewrites and rehearses her opening lines the night before, unwilling to assume that past success guarantees the same effect again.

Text 1: An excavation in Chiquihuite Cave in central Mexico has upended the belief that approximately 13,000 years ago, a group known as the Clovis people were the first human inhabitants of North America.

More than 200 crude stone tools were found embedded in a layer of earth that is up to 33,150 years old, revealing that humans occupied the cave thousands of years before the Clovis people reached the continent.
Text 2: The objects uncovered in Chiquihuite Cave are intriguing, but it is premature to characterize them as tools.
The stone pieces are so roughly shaped that they may have simply fractured from rocks during natural geological activity in the cave.
Moreover, their unearthing has thus far not been accompanied by discoveries of other signs of human activity or even traces of human DNA from surfaces.
Text 1: Newly analyzed sediment cores from a lakebed in the Andes suggest that a farming settlement existed in the region at least 2,000 years earlier than previously believed.
Researchers found layers of pollen from domesticated crops in sediment dated to that earlier period, indicating that organized agriculture began there far sooner than the standard timeline holds.
Text 2: The pollen samples from the Andean lakebed are worth further study, but it is too soon to credit them to deliberate cultivation.
The plant species identified also grow wild in the region, and the pollen could have been deposited by wind or animal activity rather than by human planting.
No accompanying evidence of tools, irrigation channels, or cleared fields has yet been found at the site.
Text 1: A set of markings on a cave wall in northern Spain has been interpreted by one research team as an early calendar tracking lunar cycles, based on the number and spacing of the marks.
If correct, this would push back the earliest known evidence of systematic timekeeping by thousands of years.
Text 2: The spacing of the marks on the cave wall is suggestive, but treating them as a calendar goes well beyond what the evidence supports.
Similar spacing patterns occur in natural rock fractures found elsewhere in the same cave system, and no other markings at the site show any consistent numerical or seasonal pattern.

Text 1: Fragments of woven fabric recovered from a bog in northern Europe have been dated to nearly 9,000 years ago, a finding one research team says proves that organized textile production began far earlier than previously thought.
Text 2: The fabric fragments are a remarkable find, but calling them evidence of organized textile production may be premature.
The fibers could have been twisted together informally, without the coordinated tools or techniques that organized production implies, and no spindles or looms have been recovered from the site.

Text 1: Scratches found on a set of ancient animal bones in East Africa have been interpreted by one team as evidence of early butchery using stone tools, pushing back the timeline for tool-assisted meat processing.
Text 2: The scratches on the bones are intriguing, but attributing them to stone-tool butchery overlooks a simpler explanation.
Trampling by other animals across sediment containing small rock fragments can produce very similar marks, and no stone tools have actually been recovered near the bones.

Text 1: Charred plant remains found at a rock shelter in Southeast Asia have been dated to a period thousands of years before the region's earliest known hearths, leading one team to argue that controlled fire use began far earlier than believed.
Text 2: The charred remains are notable, but linking them to controlled fire use is not yet warranted.
Wildfires are common in the region, and the site shows no accompanying evidence of a constructed hearth, ash management, or repeated use of a single fire location.
Many literary theorists distinguish between fabula, a narrative's content, and syuzhet, a narrative's arrangement and presentation of events.
In the film The Godfather Part II, the fabula is the story of the Corleone family, and the syuzhet is the presentation of the story as it alternates between two timelines in 1901 and 1958.

But literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin maintained that fabula and syuzhet are insufficient to completely describe a narrative—he held that systematic categorizations of artistic phenomena discount the subtle way in which meaning is created by interactions between the artist, the work, and the audience.
Many economists distinguish between supply shocks, sudden disruptions to production, and demand shocks, sudden shifts in what consumers are willing to buy.
During the region's recent fuel shortage, the supply shock was the disrupted shipment of oil, and the demand shock was the resulting shift toward alternative energy sources.

But economist Renata Kessler maintained that supply and demand shocks are insufficient to completely explain the shortage's effects—she held that standard categorizations of economic disruption discount the subtle way in which public trust in institutions shapes how quickly markets actually recover.
Many musicologists distinguish between melody, a piece's sequence of pitches, and harmony, the combination of pitches sounded together.
In a given jazz standard, the melody is the tune a listener might hum, and the harmony is the underlying chords supporting it.

But musicologist Deshawn Fields maintained that melody and harmony are insufficient to completely describe a performance—he held that standard categorizations of musical structure discount the subtle way in which a performer's timing and phrasing shape a listener's emotional experience.
Many linguists distinguish between denotation, a word's literal dictionary meaning, and connotation, the associations a word carries beyond that meaning.
In a given poem, the denotation of a word might be its plain definition, and the connotation might be the mood that word evokes.

But linguist Anya Petrenko maintained that denotation and connotation are insufficient to completely describe a word's effect in a poem—she held that standard categorizations of meaning discount the subtle way in which a word's placement and rhythm within a line shape how a reader experiences it.
Many architects distinguish between form, a building's physical shape, and function, the practical purposes the building serves.
In a given train station, the form is its arched glass roof, and the function is its role in moving passengers efficiently.

But architectural critic Soren Vik maintained that form and function are insufficient to completely describe a building's significance—he held that standard categorizations of design discount the subtle way in which a building's relationship to its surrounding neighborhood shapes how residents come to feel about it.
Many anthropologists distinguish between kinship by blood, ties based on biological descent, and kinship by practice, ties formed through shared daily life and obligation.
In a given community, kinship by blood might describe siblings, and kinship by practice might describe long-term neighbors who share caregiving duties.

But anthropologist Idris Okonjo maintained that these two categories are insufficient to completely describe how community bonds actually form—he held that standard categorizations of kinship discount the subtle way in which shared hardship over time can create obligations as strong as either category alone.

As media consumption has become increasingly multiplatform and socially mediated, active news acquisition has diminished in favor of an attitude known as "news finds me" (NFM), in which people passively rely on their social networks and ambient media environments for information about current events.

Homero Gil de Zuniga and Trevor Diehl examined data on a representative group of adults in the United States to determine participants' strength of NFM attitude, political knowledge, and political interest.

Although no major election took place sufficiently near the study for Gil de Zuniga and Diehl to identify causality between NFM and voting behavior, they did posit that NFM may reduce voting probability through an indirect effect.
Researchers Lindiwe Moyo and Aaron Kessler examined data on a group of high school students to determine each student's phone use before bed, sleep duration, and next-day academic performance.
Although no controlled sleep-lab experiment took place during the study, Moyo and Kessler posited that heavy pre-bed phone use may reduce academic performance through an indirect effect.
Researchers examined survey data from a large company to determine each employee's attitude toward the new remote-work policy, job satisfaction, and likelihood of leaving within a year.
Although no controlled trial took place during the study period, the researchers posited that positive attitudes toward remote work may reduce turnover through an indirect effect.
Researchers examined survey and crime data across several neighborhoods to determine residents' exposure to community gardens, levels of neighborly trust, and local crime rates.
Although no controlled experiment took place, the researchers posited that community garden exposure may reduce crime rates through an indirect effect.
Researchers examined data on a group of high school students to determine participation in a new mentoring program, self-confidence regarding academic ability, and eventual college enrollment.
Although no randomized trial took place, the researchers posited that mentoring program participation may increase college enrollment through an indirect effect.
Researchers examined transportation data across several cities to determine transit frequency, average traffic congestion, and traffic fatality rates.
Although no controlled experiment took place, the researchers posited that increased transit frequency may reduce fatality rates through an indirect effect.

In 2016, biological anthropologist Heather F.
Smith and her team investigated the evolution of the appendix, an intestinal organ that is present in some mammals, including humans, but is generally thought to have no function.

Studying 533 mammal species, the team found that the appendix has emerged independently across multiple lineages in separate instances and, significantly, hasn't disappeared after emerging in specific lineages.
Moreover, the team determined that species with the organ tend to have higher concentrations of lymphoid tissue, which supports immune responses, in the cecum, the organ the appendix is attached to.

In a 2019 study, biologist Rosalind Achebe and her team investigated the evolution of the spleen-adjacent "accessory lymph node" structure, an organ present in some fish species but generally thought to have no function.
Studying 240 fish species, the team found that the structure has emerged independently across multiple lineages and, significantly, hasn't disappeared after emerging in specific lineages.
Moreover, the team determined that species with the structure tend to have higher concentrations of antibody-producing cells within it.

In a 2017 study, biologist Femi Adeyemi and colleagues investigated the evolution of the plica semilunaris, a small fold of tissue in the corner of the eye present in some primates but generally thought to have no function.
Studying 180 primate species, the team found that the fold has emerged independently across multiple lineages and, significantly, hasn't disappeared after emerging in specific lineages.
Moreover, the team determined that species with the fold tend to have more effective removal of debris from the eye's surface.

In a 2021 study, biologist Talia Nowak and her team investigated the evolution of the interdigital webbing found in some rodent species, a trait generally thought to have no function outside of aquatic species.

Moreover, the team determined that species with the webbing tend to have greater digging efficiency in loose or sandy soil.

In a 2015 study, biologist Grace Okafor and colleagues investigated the evolution of the vomeronasal organ, a chemosensory structure present in some reptile species but generally thought to have no function outside of a few well-studied groups.

- Scientists have developed a "freeze-thaw" battery that can retain 92% of its charge after twelve weeks.
- The battery contains molten salt (a type of salt that liquefies when heated and solidifies at room temperature).
- When the salt is in a liquid state, energy flows through the battery.
- When the salt is in a solid state, energy stops flowing and is stored in the battery.
- The stored (frozen) energy can be used by reheating (thawing) the battery.
- Engineers have developed a "thermal latch" window coating that can retain heat for up to eight hours after sunset.
- The coating contains a wax-based compound that melts at moderate temperatures and solidifies as it cools.
- When the wax is in a liquid state, heat passes through the coating.
- When the wax is in a solid state, heat transfer slows and warmth is retained near the glass.
- The retained heat can be released back into the room once temperatures drop further.
- Scientists have developed a "pressure-lock" seal that can hold gas inside a container for months without leaking.
- The seal contains a gel-based layer that softens under pressure and stiffens once pressure is released.
- When the gel is soft, gas molecules can slowly pass through microscopic gaps.
- When the gel stiffens, the gaps close and gas is trapped inside.
- The trapped gas can be released later by reapplying pressure to soften the gel again.
- Researchers have developed a "cold-hold" battery that can retain 85% of its charge after ten weeks.
- The battery contains a wax-like electrolyte that liquefies when warmed and hardens at room temperature.
- When the electrolyte is liquid, ions move freely and the battery can charge or discharge.
- When the electrolyte hardens, ion movement stops and the charge is locked in place.
- The locked charge can be accessed again by warming the battery.
- Engineers have developed a "flow-freeze" heat exchanger that can store excess heat for later use.
- The exchanger contains a salt-based fluid that flows freely when hot and crystallizes when cooled.
- When the fluid flows, heat moves through the exchanger and is released to the surroundings.
- When the fluid crystallizes, heat movement stops and thermal energy is stored within the crystal structure.
- The stored energy can be released later by reheating the fluid.
- Scientists have developed a "damp-lock" capacitor that can hold an electrical charge for several days.
- The capacitor contains a polymer layer that absorbs moisture and swells, then dries and contracts over time.
- When the polymer is swollen, charge can move freely across the layer.
- When the polymer contracts as it dries, charge movement stops and the charge is held in place.
- The held charge can be released again once the polymer reabsorbs moisture.
